cards.front: Distinguish fusion from fission across fuel type, reaction direction, and facility maturity.
cards.back:
Fission splits heavy atoms like uranium, while fusion combines light atoms together — the same reaction that powers the sun [S2]. Existing nuclear facilities rely on fission, but fusion devices are first-of-a-kind and the industry is still experimental [S2].
• Fuel: light atoms (fusion) vs heavy atoms like uranium (fission) [S2]
cards.mnemonic: Fuse light, fission heavy — the sun does the first.
cards.source: Reuters, US roadmap targets fusion deployment by mid 2030s

cards.front: ITER is a collaboration among the United States, {{c1::the European Union (host)}}, China, India, Japan, Russia, and {{c2::South Korea}} [S1].
cards.back:
Seven partners fund ITER, with the EU as host [S1]. Europe contributes almost half of construction cost while the other six contribute equally to the remainder [S4].
• Cost split: Europe ~half; China, India, Japan, Korea, Russia, US share the rest equally [S4]
cards.mnemonic: EU hosts and pays half; six split the rest.

cards.front: What makes ITER an exploratory science project rather than a power plant?
cards.back: ITER's key goal is to operate at or near the ignition point of burning plasma and to test specialized materials, and it is not designed or intended to produce electricity [S1]. Its purpose is to develop technology for a future fusion demonstration power plant [S1].
cards.mnemonic: ITER proves the plasma, not the plug.

cards.front: ITER installed the {{c1::sixth}} of {{c2::nine}} tokamak sector modules by 29 July 2026, bringing two-thirds of the core into place [S4].
cards.back:
The module was lowered in a 30-hour lift that concluded on 28 July 2026, almost six months ahead of schedule [S4]. Three sources' agreement is stable ground here: about two-thirds of the plasma chamber was in place [S3][S4].
• Lift: ~1,100-tonne module; ~1,400 tonnes suspended with rig; 30 hours [S4]
cards.mnemonic: Six of nine down, two-thirds home, six months early.

cards.front: The sixth ITER sector module weighed about {{c1::1,100 tonnes}}; with its lifting rig the suspended load was nearly {{c2::1,400 tonnes}} [S4].
cards.back: The transfer from the Assembly Hall to the pit took 30 hours and concluded on 28 July 2026 [S4].
cards.mnemonic: Eleven hundred module, fourteen hundred with the rig.

cards.front: ITER has installed sector modules progressively since {{c1::April 2025}} and is on track to position the final module in {{c2::2027}} [S4].
cards.back: Experience from each successive module increased the pace, efficiency and predictability of the work [S4].
cards.mnemonic: April 2025 start, 2027 finish line.

cards.front: Why did ITER's sector-module installation accelerate with each successive lift?
cards.back: Lessons learned from each module assembly and lifting operation were translated into greater efficiency, stronger coordination and a more predictable sequence — ITER's accelerated approach to machine assembly [S4]. Six modules were in place almost six months ahead of schedule [S4].
cards.mnemonic: Each lift teaches the next one.

cards.front: Distinguish the two published counts of U.S. fusion companies: 28 versus 'around 30'.
cards.back:
S2 puts the figure at 28, tied to a named Fusion Industry Association 2026 dataset, while S3 says there are around 30 U.S. fusion companies [S2][S3]. The audit reads this as the same tally rounded at slightly different moments, leaning to S2's exact 28 because S3's figure is an explicit rounding.
• Count: 28 [S2] vs roughly 30 [S3]
cards.mnemonic: Twenty-eight exact, thirty a rounding.

cards.front: ITER's vacuum vessel sector 3 carries {{c1::120 sensors}} to measure {{c2::magnetic field}} during machine operation [S3].
cards.back: It is one of the most heavily instrumented vacuum vessel sectors [S3]. By summer 2026 three sectors rested on gravity supports and teams were preparing for vacuum vessel welding [S3].
cards.mnemonic: Sector three: 120 eyes on the magnetic field.

cards.front: Of ITER's nine vacuum vessel sectors, {{c1::four}} were manufactured in the Republic of Korea and {{c2::five}} in Europe [S4].
cards.back: The sixth module was built around vacuum vessel sector #1, the fourth and final sector manufactured in Korea [S4].
cards.mnemonic: Korea four, Europe five, nine sectors total.

cards.front: Why are neutron-resistant structural materials a central unsolved fusion challenge?
cards.back: Fusion components must withstand intense neutron bombardment and extreme heat, and neutron-resistant structural materials remain an agreed, unsolved engineering barrier between experimental physics and commercial net energy gain [S2].
cards.mnemonic: Neutrons chew the walls; materials must bite back.
cards.source: Reuters, US roadmap targets fusion deployment by mid 2030s

cards.front: Why do future fusion reactors need breeding blankets?
cards.back: Breeding blankets secure a steady supply of tritium, the nuclear fuel; the sources agree that future reactors are expected to rely on lithium blankets to breed their own tritium because tritium is scarce and decays [S2][S6].
cards.mnemonic: No tritium in the ground — blankets breed it.

cards.front: Distinguish the breeding blanket from neutron-resistant structural materials across problem solved and resource protected.
cards.back:
Breeding blankets solve fuel supply by breeding tritium, while neutron-resistant materials solve survival under bombardment and extreme heat [S2]. Both are named as steep engineering challenges standing between experiments and commercial net energy gain [S2].
• Both sit on the same materials-and-technology gap list [S2]
cards.mnemonic: Blanket makes the fuel; armour survives it.
cards.source: Reuters, US roadmap targets fusion deployment by mid 2030s

cards.front: Distinguish gain factor above one, engineering breakeven, and economic breakeven across what each requires.
cards.back:
As of 2025 the National Ignition Facility is the only laboratory to have demonstrated a fusion energy gain factor above one [S6]. Efficiencies orders of magnitude higher are required for engineering breakeven (a net electricity-producing plant) and economic breakeven (net electricity pays the plant's whole-life cost) [S6].
• >1 gain achieved once (NIF); both breakevens remain unmet [S6]
cards.mnemonic: One is a lab trick; breakeven pays the bills.

cards.front: What does 'net energy gain' require, and why haven't private developers reached it?
cards.back: Net energy gain is the point where a fusion reaction produces more energy than was used to start and sustain it [S2]. Private developers have not yet achieved it, and the industry remains in an experimental stage [S2].
cards.mnemonic: Out must beat in — nobody's there yet.
cards.source: Reuters, US roadmap targets fusion deployment by mid 2030s

cards.front: The DOE Fusion Science and Technology Roadmap was released in {{c1::June}} 2026, and the Office of Fusion, created in {{c2::November 2025}}, coordinates its implementation [S2].
cards.back: The roadmap is the central plank of a federal strategy to catalyze deployment of early-stage fusion power plants by the mid-2030s [S2].
cards.mnemonic: Office November, roadmap June, target mid-2030s.
cards.source: Reuters, US roadmap targets fusion deployment by mid 2030s

cards.front: DOE's fusion strategy has three goals: close materials and technology gaps, widen access to {{c1::AI and advanced computing}}, and leverage {{c2::public-private partnerships}} [S2].
cards.back: The strategy sets concrete short-, medium- and long-term milestones for structural materials, plasma-facing components and fuel processing technology [S2].
cards.mnemonic: Infrastructure, computing, partnerships — three legs.
cards.source: Reuters, US roadmap targets fusion deployment by mid 2030s

cards.front: Why does the U.S. mid-2030s fusion deployment goal hinge on federal funding?
cards.back: Industry leaders say the strategy's success hinges on more federal funding, not on milestones alone [S2]. The government launched the strategy to catalyze early-stage fusion power plant deployment by the mid-2030s [S2].
cards.mnemonic: Milestones without money are just calendar art.
cards.source: Reuters, US roadmap targets fusion deployment by mid 2030s

cards.front: Distinguish ITER from private fusion developers across mission, output, and schedule claims.
cards.back:
ITER is a science collaboration aiming at burning plasma ignition and materials testing, and is not designed or intended to produce electricity [S1]. Private developers are chasing net energy gain and grid connection, with several claiming they are on track to connect to the grid as early as the 2030s [S2][S3].
• ITER output: no electricity by design [S1]
cards.mnemonic: ITER proves physics; startups promise watts.

cards.front: The IAEA World Fusion Outlook 2025 is the {{c1::third}} issue of the publication and outlines dozens of fusion plant concepts at various stages of development worldwide [S5].
cards.back: It aims to be the global reference for authoritative information and updates on fusion energy, presenting recent achievements alongside those plant concepts [S5].
cards.mnemonic: IAEA outlook: third edition, global roll-call.

cards.front: Why could ITER teams begin preparing vacuum vessel welding in summer 2026?
cards.back: With three vacuum vessel sectors resting on their gravity supports, teams confirmed the configuration was sufficiently stable to begin welding preparations [S3]. Sector 6 had been the first transferred to its gravity support, in May 2026 [S3].
cards.mnemonic: Three on supports, stable enough to weld.

cards.front: What conditions does a fusion reaction demand of its fuel?
cards.back: Fuel must be in a plasma state inside a confined environment with high temperature, high pressure and sufficient confinement time [S6]. The source presents these as linked parameters rather than independent knobs [S6].
cards.mnemonic: Hot, dense, held long enough.
